ican.text: I can write the vector equation of a line from two distinct points or from a point and nonzero direction.
I can convert between vector and parametric forms in two or three dimensions.
I can test whether a point lies on a line by checking one consistent parameter across all components.
I can recognize equivalent line equations and restrict a parameter to represent a ray or segment.
I can distinguish a geometric line parameter from time in a motion context.

ku.text: A line in two or three dimensions can be written $\mathbf r=\mathbf a+\lambda\mathbf d$, where $\mathbf a$ is the position vector of a point on the line, $\mathbf d\ne\mathbf0$ is a direction vector and $\lambda\in\mathbb R$ for the whole line.

For distinct points $A$ and $B$, choose $\mathbf a=\overrightarrow{OA}$ and $\mathbf d=\overrightarrow{AB}=\mathbf b-\mathbf a$. Any nonzero scalar multiple of $\mathbf d$ is another valid direction vector.
If $\mathbf a=(a_1,a_2,a_3)$ and $\mathbf d=(d_1,d_2,d_3)$, the parametric equations are $x=a_1+\lambda d_1$, $y=a_2+\lambda d_2$ and $z=a_3+\lambda d_3$. The same parameter appears in all three.

To test whether $P$ lies on the line, solve a component equation for $\lambda$ where the direction component is nonzero, then substitute that same value into every remaining component. If a direction component is zero, the corresponding coordinate must match the fixed coordinate.

Different equations can describe the same line: choose another point on it and any nonzero multiple of the direction. To establish equivalence, check that the directions are parallel and a point from one line lies on the other.

With $\mathbf d=\mathbf b-\mathbf a$, the segment from $A$ to $B$ has $0\leq\lambda\leq1$ and the ray starting at $A$ towards $B$ has $\lambda\geq0$. If the direction is rescaled, the parameter values for $B$ and the segment bounds must be rescaled too.

For an intersection of two lines, use independent parameters and equate corresponding components. A consistent pair yields an intersection point; an inconsistent system does not. In three dimensions nonparallel lines can be skew and fail to intersect.
A parameter is not automatically time or distance. If a motion model defines $t$ as time, the direction coefficient is velocity only when its units and linear model support that interpretation.

misc.weak: Use the endpoint $B$ as the direction vector.
misc.better: A direction vector is a displacement such as $\mathbf b-\mathbf a$, unless the given vector is explicitly a direction.

misc.weak: The same point can use different parameter values in different components.
misc.better: A point on a line must satisfy all component equations using one common parameter value.

misc.weak: A line and segment have the same unrestricted parameter domain.
misc.better: A full line uses all real parameters; a segment requires bounds tied to the chosen direction vector.

misc.weak: Any two nonparallel lines in three dimensions intersect.
misc.better: They may be skew. Solve all three component equations to check consistency.

misc.weak: The direction vector must have magnitude one.
misc.better: Any nonzero scalar multiple gives the same line; normalizing is optional unless requested.

formula.text: Vector line: $\mathbf r=\mathbf a+\lambda\mathbf d$, where $\mathbf d\ne\mathbf0$ and $\lambda\in\mathbb R$.
Parametric form: $x=a_1+\lambda d_1$, $y=a_2+\lambda d_2$, and in three dimensions $z=a_3+\lambda d_3$.

worked.prompt: In three-dimensional space, let $A=(1,-1,2)$ and $B=(5,1,0)$. Consider the line through $A$ and $B$.

parts.label: a
parts.q: Find a vector equation of the line and write its parametric equations.
parts.a: $\overrightarrow{AB}=(4,2,-2)=2(2,1,-1)$. One equation is $\mathbf r=(1,-1,2)+\lambda(2,1,-1)$, $\lambda\in\mathbb R$. Thus $x=1+2\lambda$, $y=-1+\lambda$ and $z=2-\lambda$.

parts.label: b
parts.q: Determine whether $C=(7,2,-1)$ and $D=(3,0,2)$ lie on the line.
parts.a: For $C$, the first component gives $\lambda=3$; the other components give $y=2$, $z=-1$, so $C$ lies on the line. For $D$, the first component gives $\lambda=1$, which predicts $z=1$, not $2$. Therefore $D$ is not on the line.

parts.label: c
parts.q: Using the equation from part (a), give the parameter range for the segment from $A$ to $B$.
parts.a: $A$ occurs at $\lambda=0$. Since $B-A=2(2,1,-1)$, $B$ occurs at $\lambda=2$. The segment is $0\leq\lambda\leq2$.

parts.label: d
parts.q: Show that $\mathbf r=(7,2,-1)+\mu(-4,-2,2)$ represents the same line.
parts.a: The new starting point is $C$, which lies on the original line, and $(-4,-2,2)=-2(2,1,-1)$ is a nonzero multiple of its direction. Therefore the two equations represent the same full line.

parts.label: e
parts.q: A second line is $\mathbf r=(3,0,1)+\mu(1,-1,2)$. Find its intersection with the original line.
parts.a: Equate components: $1+2\lambda=3+\mu$, $-1+\lambda=-\mu$ and $2-\lambda=1+2\mu$. The first two give $\lambda=1$, $\mu=0$; these also satisfy the third. The intersection is $(3,0,1)$.

kq.q: Why do different direction vectors describe the same line?
kq.model: Any nonzero scalar multiple is parallel to the original direction. The parameter changes its scale or sign to reach the same points.

kq.q: Why must the same parameter work in every coordinate?
kq.model: The parameter selects a single point on the line. Different values in different coordinates would mix components of different points.

kq.q: Why can two nonparallel lines in space fail to meet?
kq.model: They can pass in different planes without sharing a point. Equating all three coordinates tests whether one consistent pair of parameters exists.

kq.q: Why do segment bounds depend on the chosen direction?
kq.model: Rescaling the direction rescales the parameter needed to reach an endpoint. Calculate the parameter values of both endpoints for the particular equation.
